records.title: Enterprise AI use is shifting from assistance to agentic execution

records.title: CFO revenue-growth expectations for 2026 and 2027
records.finding: In the Q3 survey, respondents expected mean year-over-year revenue growth of 7.7% for calendar 2026 and 7.2% for 2027; the median expectation was 5.0% in both years.
records.coverage: The growth-expectation table covers 463 to 506 U.S. firms, depending on the metric; revenue responses are sales-revenue weighted and winsorized at 5%. The overall survey included 517 financial executives.
records.period: Survey fielded August 17-September 4, 2026; expectations for calendar 2026 and 2027.

source.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Duke University and Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta
source.title: The CFO Survey Q3 2026: Data and Results

records.title: Financial constraints affecting small and large firms
records.finding: Twenty percent of small firms reported financial constraints that prevented them from covering costs or pursuing new business opportunities, compared with about 10% of large firms.
records.coverage: 517 financial executives participated overall; the public source does not state the small- and large-firm subgroup counts.
records.period: Survey fielded August 17-September 4, 2026; current financial constraints.
records.type: U.S. CFO survey response by firm size

records.title: Interest rates and potential hikes among top CFO concerns
records.finding: Twenty percent of decision-makers named current interest rates or the potential for future rate hikes among their top concerns.
records.coverage: 517 financial executives participated overall; the public source does not state the response count for this question.
records.period: Survey fielded August 17-September 4, 2026; current business concerns.

source.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Duke University and Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta
source.title: The CFO Survey: High Interest Rates and Rising Labor Costs Weigh on CFOs

records.title: Time to expected value for simpler finance AI use cases
records.finding: Finance AI use cases involving data extraction, accounts-payable and accounts-receivable automation, and report creation generally delivered returns within nine to 10 months.
records.coverage: 160 senior finance-function leaders.
records.period: Survey conducted January-April 2026; reported time to expected value.

source.title: Gartner Says CFOs Must Take a More Disciplined Approach to Finance AI

records.title: Threats to finance-function stability entering 2027
records.finding: Half of respondents named the talent and skills gap as the single greatest threat to finance-function stability over the coming year, compared with shifting regulation at 21%, cyber and AI-driven fraud at 16%, and macroeconomic volatility at 14%.
records.coverage: 116 senior-level financial and accounting executives, including CFOs, controllers, chief accounting officers, and finance vice presidents, predominantly from U.S. organizations; the public source does not state field dates.
records.period: Current assessment for the coming year; public source does not state field dates.

records.title: Senior finance time spent on manual data work and close duration
records.finding: Thirty-six percent reported that directors, controllers, and senior managers spend 31% to 50% of their time firefighting and performing manual data intervention; 40% reported a monthly close of seven days or longer.
records.coverage: 116 senior-level financial and accounting executives, including CFOs, controllers, chief accounting officers, and finance vice presidents, predominantly from U.S. organizations; the public source does not state field dates.
records.period: Current finance-function practices; public source does not state field dates.

records.title: Finance AI spending plans, strategic integration, and impact measurement
records.finding: Fifty-three percent planned to direct a significant or substantial portion of their technology budget to AI over the next 12 to 24 months; 3% described AI as core and strategically integrated, while 39% were deploying AI without a formal impact-measurement framework.
records.coverage: 116 senior-level financial and accounting executives, including CFOs, controllers, chief accounting officers, and finance vice presidents, predominantly from U.S. organizations; the public source does not state field dates.
records.period: Current AI practices and plans for the next 12-24 months; public source does not state field dates.

records.title: Finance-team reskilling investment
records.finding: Ten percent of organizations reported investing aggressively in reskilling their finance teams, while 11% reported investing nothing.
records.coverage: 116 senior-level financial and accounting executives, including CFOs, controllers, chief accounting officers, and finance vice presidents, predominantly from U.S. organizations; the public source does not state field dates.
records.period: Current workforce investment; public source does not state field dates.

records.title: Human control over AI-assisted finance decisions
records.finding: Thirty-two percent reported using AI to recommend actions that teams execute manually, while 29% allowed AI to act with human approval.
records.coverage: 338 finance leaders: 137 CFOs in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and Canada, plus 201 director-level and above finance leaders in the United States and United Kingdom.
records.period: Survey fielded in August 2026; current AI decision practices.

records.title: Reported finance AI productivity and cash-flow benefits
records.finding: Fifty-eight percent of finance leaders reported productivity gains from AI, and 48% reported stronger cash flow.
records.coverage: 338 finance leaders: 137 CFOs in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and Canada, plus 201 director-level and above finance leaders in the United States and United Kingdom.
records.period: Survey fielded in August 2026; reported current outcomes.

records.title: AI spending overruns, software costs, and outcome attribution
records.finding: Seventy-two percent reported spending more on AI than planned during the prior 12 months. Among CFOs, 75% reported increased software and subscription costs, compared with 45% of other finance leaders, and 65% had difficulty linking AI use to outcomes, compared with 40% of other finance leaders.
records.coverage: 338 finance leaders: 137 CFOs in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and Canada, plus 201 director-level and above finance leaders in the United States and United Kingdom.
records.period: Survey fielded in August 2026; AI spending during the prior 12 months and current outcome attribution.
records.type: Cross-market finance-leader survey response with CFO subgroup comparison

records.title: Data quality and integration barriers to expanding finance AI
records.finding: Forty-eight percent cited data quality and 42% cited insufficient integration as barriers to expanding AI; integration was cited by 58% of CFOs, compared with 31% of other finance leaders.
records.coverage: 338 finance leaders: 137 CFOs in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and Canada, plus 201 director-level and above finance leaders in the United States and United Kingdom.
records.period: Survey fielded in August 2026; current barriers to expanding AI.
records.type: Cross-market finance-leader survey response with CFO subgroup comparison

records.title: Unapproved AI use within finance
records.finding: Sixty-six percent of finance leaders knew or suspected that finance employees were using unapproved AI tools.
records.coverage: 338 finance leaders: 137 CFOs in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and Canada, plus 201 director-level and above finance leaders in the United States and United Kingdom.
records.period: Survey fielded in August 2026; current AI-governance observation.
